summary:
Isparta province stands under the national framework of Turkey. The sources behind this record contain no Isparta-specific statute, incident, police action or court case, so the assessment below sets out national law and national enforcement as they apply in Isparta alongside every other province.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend Turkey's penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality at up to three years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies at up to four years. The same package would raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25, condition it on infertility and repeated evaluations, and expose medical providers to fines and up to seven years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to it.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025. Had they entered force they would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was ultimately submitted to parliament. The absence of enacted statutes has not restrained enforcement: the report describes 2025 as an unprecedented assault on LGBTI people in legislative form.

Public assembly is the sharpest point of contact between a trans visitor and Turkish policing. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned an Istanbul governorate ban as disproportionate and unlawful, yet prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, finding that it had acted outside its stated purpose and shared obscene images incompatible with the law. Istanbul and Izmir stand here as examples of a pattern the sources record nationally rather than as isolated local events.

The baseline law is more permissive than the enforcement climate. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive statute prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 request to include it in constitutional drafting was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP.

One further measure was under consideration as of February 2026, when a newspaper reported that the government was weighing a law criminalising the public encouragement of "behavior contrary to biological sex" with a sentence of one to three years. Its status is a press report rather than a published draft, and the sources do not say whether it progressed.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between pending legislation and present policing is the central turbulence in the record. Draft packages that were never submitted to parliament nonetheless accompany blanket bans, arbitrary detentions, ongoing prosecutions and the dissolution of an LGBTI association, which means a visitor cannot read the unpassed status of a bill as an absence of risk.

Pride bans have recurred across multiple provinces for most years, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against participants who defied them. The governors of Istanbul, Izmir and Antalya banned the 27th Istanbul Pride, the 7th Izmir Pride and the 3rd Antalya Pride on 14 June 2019, placing assembly restrictions among the longest-running features of the regime rather than a response to any single year.

The historical baseline cuts the other way. Decriminalisation of homosexuality dates to 1858 and legal gender change to 1988, both well before the current legislative drive, so the direction of travel runs against a long-standing formal legality rather than reversing it.

For a trans visitor, the practical comparison is between what the statute book says and what a checkpoint, a march or a street stop produces. The sources support the second and give limited comfort from the first.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Turkey since 1988, and the sources describe no Isparta-specific procedure, court or medical board governing it. Residents seeking recognition do so under national rules that apply uniformly across provinces.

Openly LGBT people are barred from military service. The armed forces' health regulation classifies homosexuality as a psychosexual illness rendering members unfit, and conscripts who declare homosexuality must supply photographic proof. This provision bears on residents subject to conscription and does not apply to visitors.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2012 constitutional-writing request to include same-sex marriage was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP.

Organising carries direct exposure. The Izmir court's December 2025 dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association and the 92 pride-related prosecutions still running at year's end show that association and participation, not only identity, attract state action.

Domestic opposition to the 11th Judicial Package comes from fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association, whose objections are recorded in the sources alongside the draft's contents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Isparta-specific source appears in this inventory: no local statute, police action, court case, health facility or incident involving a trans person in Isparta province is documented. The province-level assessment rests entirely on national material and should be read that way.

The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is stated only as of the Human Rights Watch release of 29 October 2025. Whether it has since been tabled, amended or abandoned is unresolved in the sources.

The February 2026 measure is sourced to a newspaper report rather than a published draft text. Its existence, contents and current status remain unresolved.

Whether the June 2025 Istanbul pride bans or the Izmir dissolution order have been appealed or overturned beyond the November 2025 ruling on the Istanbul governorate ban is not sourced here. The fate of the 92 prosecutions after year-end is likewise unresolved.

The sources give no figures for Isparta on detentions, hate incidents or access to transition-related care, so the absence of recorded events in the province should not be read as evidence that none occurred.
